text: Can you describe exactly how your right leg is positioned compared to your left one, and are you experiencing any numbness or tingling? Please tell me if you have any pain in your lower back or buttocks as well.

speaker: Patient
text: 25-year-old female. The patient was involved in a rear-end collision where she was the restrained driver of the back car. She reports immediate onset of pain in both knees and severe pain over the right groin area following the accident.

speaker: Doctor
text: Doctor: Is your right leg currently resting in an externally rotated and shortened position compared to your left leg? Can you tell me if you are able to move your right foot or toes at all?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Severe right groin pain. I also have Pain in both knees, Right leg is slightly shortened, flexed, adducted, and internally rotated.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the mechanism of injury and the specific positioning of your leg being shortened, adducted, and internally rotated, I strongly suspect an anterior hip dislocation. To confirm this and rule out a fracture, I need to see the imaging immediately. REQUEST IMAGES: Pelvis and Hip X-Ray.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical history. Social history: Works as an elementary school teacher. Non-smoker and drinks alcohol socially.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you have any numbness or tingling in your right leg, and can you feel your foot moving? Have you been able to urinate since the accident?

speaker: Doctor
text: I need to clarify if you are experiencing any numbness, tingling, or loss of sensation in your right leg or foot. Additionally, have you been able to urinate normally since the accident, or do you have any difficulty emptying your bladder?

speaker: Doctor
text: Since your leg is shortened, adducted, and internally rotated, I suspect a posterior hip dislocation rather than an anterior one, and I need to confirm this immediately. REQUEST IMAGES: Pelvis and Hip X-Ray.

text: The X-ray confirms a posterior hip dislocation with an associated femoral head fracture. Given the severity and the risk of avascular necrosis, I must proceed with immediate reduction. DIAGNOSIS READY: Posterior Hip Dislocation with Femoral Head Fracture.
